This upfront investment of expertise can yield highly actionable models, but it underscores that successful ML is deeply reliant on the fusion of data science techniques with domain-specific human intelligence. 2.3 Many Tools: From Simple Baselines to Advanced Ensembles To accomplish the tasks of prediction and classification, the process engineer can draw from a diverse arsenal of ML algorithms. Each algorithm possesses a unique internal logic, making it better suited for certain types of data and problems. This section provides a curated tour of the key algorithms that proved effective across the five case studies of this report, organized by their complexity and ideal use case. The varied success of these distinct algorithms is not arbitrary; it demonstrates that the selection of a model is an implicit hypothesis about the underlying structure of the data. Integration of Data Driven Process Control for Maximizing Energy and Resource Efficiency in WRRFs 11 2.3.1 An Indispensable Baseline: Linear Regression The simplest and most interpretable starting point for any modeling endeavor is often a Linear Regression model. This method finds the "best-fit line" (or hyperplane in multiple dimensions) that describes the relationship between input features and a continuous output variable. Its primary value in a modern ML workflow is to serve as a crucial baseline. If a more complex, "black-box" model cannot significantly outperform a simple linear model, the added complexity is likely not justified. In this project, linear models were explored in several applications. For the carbon diversion case study (Application 1), however, a simple linear model was found to be consistently inaccurate, a clear case of underfitting, where the model is too simplistic to capture the complex, nonlinear dynamics of the system. 2.3.2 Versatility: Tree-Based Ensembles (Random Forest & XGBoost) For many problems involving tabular data—the rows and columns of sensor readings and lab results common in a WRRF—tree-based ensemble models are the versatile workhorses. These models can be intuitively understood as highly optimized flowcharts composed of a multitude of "if-then" decisions (Hastie et al. 2009). Their power lies in their ability to automatically capture complex, nonlinear interactions between features without requiring extensive data preprocessing like feature scaling. Two prominent examples are Random Forest and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). 2.3.3 eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) XGBoost was a standout performer across this project's Applications. It is an advanced implementation of the gradient boosting framework, which builds decision trees sequentially. Each new tree is trained to correct the errors, or residuals, of the preceding ones (Chen and Guestrin 2016). XGBoost enhances this process with built-in regularization to control model complexity and prevent overfitting, as well as numerous optimizations for computational speed and efficiency (Chen and Guestrin 2016).
